why: Organic search brings visitors you do not pay for each click, often the largest traffic source of a website. Almost every marketing job asks for SEO basics, and SEO specialists are hired on their own.
outcome: explain crawling, indexing and ranking, choose keywords by intent, write titles and descriptions, read robots.txt and canonical tags, check Core Web Vitals, plan links and measure results in Google Search Console.

lessons.title: How search engines work
text: A search engine does three things. It crawls: robots (Googlebot) follow links and download pages. It indexes: it reads each page, understands its topic and stores it. It ranks: for each query, it orders the indexed pages by how useful they are likely to be.
A page can fail at each step: not found (no links to it), not indexed (blocked, duplicate, low quality) or indexed but ranked too low to be seen. SEO work starts by finding which step fails.
points: No crawl, no index; no index, no ranking.
Google ranks pages, not websites: each page targets its own queries.
Ranking signals include relevance, quality, links, page experience and freshness when it matters.
Google’s guidance: write helpful content for people first (E-E-A-T: experience, expertise, authoritativeness, trust).

lessons.title: Keyword research and search intent
text: Keyword research finds the words your audience types, how often (volume), how hard it is to rank (difficulty) and what they want (intent). Tools: Google Search Console, Google Keyword Planner, Semrush, Ahrefs, or simply Google’s suggestions and 'People also ask'.

Intent matters more than volume. Informational queries want an answer, commercial ones compare options, transactional ones want to buy, navigational ones look for a brand. Look at the current first page: it shows which kind of page Google thinks answers the query.
points: Long-tail keywords (longer, precise) have less volume but convert better and are easier.
Group keywords by topic: one page per intent, not one page per keyword.
Two pages targeting the same query compete with each other (cannibalization).
Check the first results before writing: a guide will not rank where Google shows product pages.

example.code:
Keyword                              Volume/month  Difficulty  Intent
running shoes                        90,000        very high   mixed
best running shoes for flat feet     2,400         medium      commercial
running shoes flat feet women        880           low         commercial
how to know if you have flat feet    1,900         low         informational
stridelab arch 3 review              140           low         transactional
example.note: The broad term is out of reach for a small site; the precise commercial queries are the realistic targets.

lessons.title: On-page SEO: titles, descriptions and content
text: The title tag is the clickable line in search results and a strong relevance signal: put the main keyword near the start, keep it around 50–60 characters, and make it attractive. The meta description does not change ranking but often becomes the snippet: around 150–160 characters that make people click.

On the page: one H1 that says what the page is about, subheadings (H2, H3) that structure it, the answer early, descriptive alt text on images, short readable URLs, and internal links to related pages with descriptive anchor text.
points: Write the title for the person searching, not only for the robot.
Each page needs a unique title and description.
Cover the topic fully: the questions the reader will ask next.
Update pages that lose traffic rather than writing new ones on the same topic.

example.code:
<head>
  <title>Running Shoes for Flat Feet: 2026 Guide | StrideLab</title>
  <meta name="description" content="Compare 12 running shoes tested on flat feet: support, cushioning and price. Free size guide and 30-day returns.">
  <link rel="canonical" href="https://stridelab.example/guides/running-shoes-flat-feet">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
</head>
example.note: Title with the keyword first and the brand last; a description that promises a concrete benefit.

lessons.title: Technical SEO: crawling and indexing
text: robots.txt tells robots which paths not to crawl; it does not remove a page from the index. To keep a page out of results, use a noindex meta tag (and let robots crawl it so they can see the tag). An XML sitemap lists the pages you want indexed and helps robots find them.

The canonical tag tells search engines which URL is the main version when several URLs show the same content (filters, tracking parameters, http and https). Redirect moved pages with a 301 (permanent) redirect, and fix broken links that return 404.
points: Blocking a page in robots.txt and adding noindex at the same time does not work: the robot never sees the noindex.
Use HTTPS everywhere and one version of the domain (with or without www).
Mobile-first indexing: Google mainly uses the mobile version of the page.
Search Console → Pages shows which pages are indexed and why others are not.

example.code:
# https://stridelab.example/robots.txt
User-agent: *
Disallow: /cart/
Disallow: /search?

Sitemap: https://stridelab.example/sitemap.xml
example.note: The cart and the internal search results are not worth crawling; the sitemap address helps robots find everything else.

lessons.title: Page experience and Core Web Vitals
text: Core Web Vitals measure how a page feels to real users: Largest Contentful Paint (LCP, loading: the main content appears within 2.5 s), Interaction to Next Paint (INP, responsiveness: under 200 ms; it replaced First Input Delay in March 2024) and Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS, visual stability: under 0.1).

Measure them with PageSpeed Insights and the Core Web Vitals report in Search Console, which use field data from Chrome users. Common fixes: compress and size images, load less JavaScript, reserve space for images and ads, use a CDN and caching.
points: Field data (real users) is what counts; lab tests help find the cause.
A threshold is 'good' when 75 % of visits meet it.
Speed also improves conversion, not only SEO.
Fast pages do not beat relevant ones: experience is a tie-breaker, content comes first.

lessons.title: Links, local SEO and structured data
text: Links from other websites act as votes of confidence: a few links from relevant, trusted sites are worth more than many from weak ones. Earn them with content people want to cite: studies, tools, guides, data. Buying links breaks Google’s spam policies and can get a site demoted.

For a local business, the Google Business Profile (address, opening hours, photos, reviews) drives the map results. Structured data (schema.org in JSON-LD) describes products, reviews, events or FAQs so search engines can show rich results such as stars and prices.
points: Internal links spread authority inside your own site: link your important pages often.
Ask satisfied customers for reviews and answer them, positive or negative.
Keep name, address and phone identical everywhere (NAP consistency).
Test structured data with Google’s Rich Results Test.

example.note: Product structured data: name, rating and offer. Only mark up what is visible on the page.

lessons.title: Measuring SEO and reporting
text: Google Search Console is the free source of truth for Google Search: impressions, clicks, average position and click-through rate by query and by page, indexing problems and Core Web Vitals. Web analytics (such as GA4) shows what organic visitors do next: sign-ups, purchases.
SEO is slow: changes take weeks to show. Report trends over months, compare like with like (same period last year for seasonal businesses) and link SEO to business results, not only rankings.
points: High impressions with low CTR: rewrite the title and description.
Position 5–15 queries are the quickest wins: improve those pages.
Annotate releases and Google updates to explain changes.
An SEO audit lists problems by impact and effort, not as one long list.

lessons.title: Working in a CMS: WordPress and the HTML you must read
text: Most junior marketing jobs do not ask you to code, but they do ask you to publish: “WordPress”, “CMS” or “back office” appear in many offers. WordPress runs a large share of the web, and its words are worth knowing. Pages are timeless (About, Contact, a service page); posts are dated articles, sorted into categories and tags and listed on the blog. Permalinks (Settings → Permalinks) decide what URLs look like: choose “Post name” so a URL reads /running-shoes-flat-feet/, not /?p=123, and decide it before launch, because changing it later changes every URL. The block editor builds a page from blocks (heading, paragraph, image, list), and the Media Library is where each image gets its alt text.

WordPress handles the basics, and an SEO plugin such as Yoast SEO or Rank Math adds a box under each page. There you set the SEO title (the <title> shown in results), the meta description, the URL slug, the canonical URL and whether the page may be indexed. The plugin also builds the XML sitemap (Yoast and Rank Math both serve one at /sitemap_index.xml), which you then submit in Search Console. One setting to check on every new site: Settings → Reading → “Discourage search engines from indexing this site”. It is ticked on many test sites and, if it stays ticked at launch, it asks search engines to keep the whole site out of their results.

Other platforms use the same ideas with other menus. Shopify (online shops), Wix and Webflow (showcase sites) all let you edit the SEO title, meta description, URL and image alt text of a page, and they generate the sitemap themselves. Learn where these fields are on the platform your employer uses; the SEO thinking does not change.

Whatever the CMS, what Google reads is the HTML. A marketer should recognise these lines: (the clickable title), <meta name="description"> (the snippet), <meta name="robots" content="noindex"> (keep out of results), <link rel="canonical"> (the main URL), <link rel="alternate" hreflang="fr"> (the same page in another language or country), the headings <h1> to <h3>, <img alt="…"> and links <a href="…">. A paid or affiliate link carries rel="sponsored", a link added by users (comments, forums) rel="ugc", and a link you do not want to vouch for rel="nofollow".

To check a page, open its source: Ctrl+U (Cmd+Option+U on a Mac) or type view-source: before the address, then search (Ctrl+F) for <title, canonical, robots. Right-click → Inspect shows the page after JavaScript has run, which can differ from the source. Ask a developer when the fix is in the theme or the templates (a canonical wrong on every product page, a missing H1 everywhere), for redirects, robots.txt, site speed or structured data the plugin does not cover. Give them the URL, the line you found and the line you expect: that is a ticket they can fix in minutes.
points: Pages are timeless, posts are dated and sorted into categories; set permalinks to “Post name” before launch.
Yoast or Rank Math: SEO title, meta description, slug, canonical, indexing and the XML sitemap.
After launch, check that “Discourage search engines” is not ticked and that the home page has no noindex.
Paid or affiliate links: rel="sponsored"; user links: rel="ugc"; links you do not vouch for: rel="nofollow".
View source (Ctrl+U) shows the HTML sent; Inspect shows the page after JavaScript.

example.code:
Running shoes for flat feet: 12 pairs tested

Our top 3 for beginners

Buy the Stride X2
example.note: What a marketer checks in a page’s source: one clear title and description, indexable, a canonical pointing to itself, hreflang for the English and French versions, one H1, alt text on the image and rel="sponsored" on the paid link.

lessons.title: AI search: AI Overviews, AI Mode and being cited
text: Search results now often start with an answer written by AI. Google shows AI Overviews (a summary at the top of the results, with links to its sources) and AI Mode (a conversation-style search where you ask follow-up questions). Chat assistants also search the web and cite pages: ChatGPT search, Perplexity, Microsoft Copilot. For a marketer, two things change: some questions are answered without a click, and being one of the cited sources becomes a new kind of visibility. The field moves fast: features, names and countries change from month to month, so check the official pages before you promise anything.

What Google says publicly (Search Central, “AI features and your website”): the same SEO best practices apply. A page must be indexed and eligible to be shown with a snippet in Google Search to be used as a source; there is no extra requirement, no special markup and no special AI file needed. Google’s advice is to keep doing the basics: let Googlebot crawl the page, write helpful, reliable, people-first content, make important content available as text, give a good page experience and make sure structured data matches what is visible on the page. The usual snippet controls (nosnippet, max-snippet, data-nosnippet) also limit what can be shown in these AI features.

Measuring is harder. Google states that traffic from AI features is counted in Search Console’s Performance report, in the “Web” search type, together with the rest of Google Search; you cannot filter it out on its own. So keep reading the usual signals (impressions, clicks, CTR by query and page) and add your own: visits from chat assistants in GA4 referrals (for example chatgpt.com or perplexity.ai), branded searches and conversions. Be careful with tools that promise an “AI ranking”: answers change with each question and each person.

Pages that get cited tend to make the answer easy to find and easy to trust: a direct answer near the top, then the detail; clear headings that match the questions people ask; tables and lists; original data (your own tests, surveys, prices); an author and a date; and a brand that is mentioned elsewhere (press, reviews, forums). None of this is new: it is good SEO and good writing, and it also helps the people who still click.

Generative AI is also a writing tool. Google’s position is that using AI to create content is not against its rules if the content is helpful and original; what is spam is “scaled content abuse”: producing many pages mainly to manipulate rankings, without value for the reader, however they are produced. In practice: use AI for outlines, first drafts and translations, then have a person check every fact, add real experience and data, and keep the pages people need, not the pages a keyword list suggests. Never publish an AI text you have not read.
points: AI Overviews and AI Mode use pages that are indexed and eligible for a snippet: no special markup or AI file is needed.
Helpful, reliable, people-first content, crawlable and in text: the same fundamentals as before.
Search Console counts AI feature traffic in the Performance report (Web search type), not separately.
Easy to cite: answer first, clear headings, tables, original data, author and date, brand mentions.
AI-written content is fine if helpful and checked by a person; mass pages made to rank are scaled content abuse.

example.code:
Query: are running shoes for flat feet worth it

Page that tends to be easy to quote:
  H1   Running shoes for flat feet: 12 pairs tested
  1st paragraph (the answer)
       Yes, if your arch collapses when you run: in our test of 12 pairs,
       stability shoes reduced inward rolling for 9 of our 14 testers.
  H2   How we tested (method, dates, testers)
  H2   Our picks by budget (table: model, price, weight, verdict)
  H2   When you do not need them
  Author box: physiotherapist, sports clinic, updated 2026-10

Page that is hard to quote:
  H1   The ultimate guide
  600 words of introduction before any answer, no date, no author,
  no data of its own, the same text as 50 other sites
example.note: The first page answers the question in its first lines, shows its own data and method, and says who wrote it and when: easy for a person and for an AI answer to quote. The second page has nothing a summary would need to cite.

items: Robots follow links and download pages
The page is read, understood and stored
Indexed pages are ordered for each query
Clickable title in results, ~50–60 characters, keyword first
Snippet text, ~150–160 characters, no ranking effect
One main heading that says what the page is about
Describes an image for screen readers and search engines
Link to another page of your site with a descriptive anchor
Paths robots should not crawl (not de-indexing)
Meta tag that keeps a page out of results
Permanent move, passes signals to the new URL
List of the pages you want indexed
The page reacts fast to clicks and taps
Queries, clicks, positions, indexing, Core Web Vitals
Speed and Core Web Vitals of one page
Timeless pages (About, services) vs dated articles in categories
URL format; choose “Post name” before launch
SEO title, meta description, canonical, noindex, XML sitemap
On paid and affiliate links (rel="ugc" for user links)
Same page in another language or country
Google’s AI answers; sources must be indexed and snippet-eligible
Many pages made to rank, without value: spam, AI or not

pitfalls: Chasing a broad keyword a small site cannot rank for, instead of precise long-tail queries.
Using robots.txt to hide a page from results (use noindex).
Several pages targeting the same query and competing with each other.
Buying links or stuffing keywords: both break Google’s spam policies.
Reporting rankings only, without clicks, conversions and revenue.
Launching a WordPress site with “Discourage search engines from indexing this site” still ticked.

exercises.q: Which search has commercial intent (the person compares options before buying)?
options: how to know if you have flat feet
best running shoes for flat feet
exercises.answer: “Best … for …” compares products before a purchase: commercial intent. The two “how / what” searches are informational, “stridelab login” is navigational.

exercises.q: Tap the line that will keep this page out of Google’s results.
exercises.snippet:
<head>
  <title>Home</title>
  <meta name="description" content="Compare 12 running shoes tested on flat feet.">
  <meta name="robots" content="noindex">
  <link rel="canonical" href="https://stridelab.example/guides/running-shoes-flat-feet">
</head>
exercises.answer: noindex asks search engines not to show the page. It is often left over from a test site. Remove it (or use index, follow). The title “Home” is weak too: it should describe the page.

exercises.q: Match each Core Web Vital with what it measures.
pairs: How fast the main content appears
How fast the page reacts to a click or tap
Whether elements jump while the page loads
exercises.answer: Largest Contentful Paint (good: ≤ 2.5 s), Interaction to Next Paint (≤ 200 ms) and Cumulative Layout Shift (≤ 0.1).

exercises.q: Put the steps in the order a page goes through before it can bring visitors from Google.
steps: Googlebot finds a link to the page
The page ranks for a query
exercises.answer: Discovery, crawl, index, rank, click. When a page brings no traffic, find which step fails first (Search Console → URL inspection).

exercises.q: A product page exists at two URLs (with and without ?color=blue). Which tag tells Google the main URL?
exercises.answer: The canonical tag, <link rel="canonical" href="…">, on both versions, pointing to the main URL.

exercises.q: A blog page has 40,000 impressions a month in Search Console, an average position of 4 and a CTR of 0.8 %. What do you do?

steps.text: What is the first thing you look at?

choices.label: The title and description shown in results
choices.feedback: At position 4 a CTR under 1 % is low: the snippet does not make people click.

choices.label: Buy links to reach position 1
choices.feedback: Buying links breaks Google’s spam policies, and the problem here is the click, not the position.

choices.label: Delete the page
choices.feedback: The page already ranks well; deleting it loses the impressions.

steps.text: The title is “Blog post 12”. What do you change?

choices.label: A title with the query and a clear benefit, plus a description that answers the intent
choices.feedback: Then compare the CTR over the next 4 weeks in Search Console.

choices.label: Repeat the keyword five times in the title
choices.feedback: Keyword stuffing reads badly and does not earn clicks.

exercises.answer: Low CTR at a good position means the snippet is the problem: rewrite the title and description for the query’s intent, then measure the CTR change in Search Console.

exercises.q: You start SEO for a local bakery in Tunis. List five actions, in the order you would do them.
exercises.answer: 1) Create and complete the Google Business Profile (address, hours, photos, category). 2) Make sure the site is indexed, fast and mobile-friendly (Search Console, PageSpeed Insights). 3) Give each product family and the shop page a clear title and description with the city (“Pâtisserie à Tunis …”). 4) Ask happy customers for reviews and answer them. 5) Get mentioned by local sites (press, guides, partners) and keep name, address and phone identical everywhere.

exercises.q: Tap the line in this <head> that sends Google to the wrong main URL.
exercises.snippet:
<head>
  <title>Running shoes for flat feet: 12 pairs tested | StrideLab</title>
  <meta name="description" content="We tested 12 running shoes on flat feet. Our picks by budget and distance.">
  <link rel="canonical" href="https://staging.stridelab.example/guides/running-shoes-flat-feet">
  <link rel="alternate" hreflang="en" href="https://stridelab.example/guides/running-shoes-flat-feet">
  <link rel="alternate" hreflang="fr" href="https://stridelab.example/fr/guides/chaussures-running-pieds-plats">
</head>
exercises.answer: The canonical points to the staging (test) site, so Google is told the main version lives on a site that should not be in results. It often happens when a site is copied from staging to production. The canonical should point to the live URL, usually the page itself.

exercises.q: Match each HTML element with its role.
pairs: The clickable title in search results
The text often shown under the title
The main URL among duplicate pages
The same page in another language
Describes an image for screen readers and search engines
Marks a paid or affiliate link
exercises.answer: Six lines to know by heart: you will check them in the SEO plugin and in the page source on almost every page you publish.

exercises.q: Sort these ways of using generative AI for content.

groups.name: Good practice
items: Use AI for an outline, then write with your own test data
Have an expert check every fact before publishing
Draft a translation with AI, then have a native speaker review it

groups.name: Risky or spam
items: Publish 500 city pages that differ only by the city name
Copy competitors’ articles and have AI rephrase them
Publish AI answers without reading them

exercises.answer: Google judges the content, not the tool: AI is fine when a person adds value and checks it. Mass pages made to rank, rewritten copies and unread texts are what its spam policies call scaled content abuse.

exercises.q: According to Google’s guidance, what does a page need to be eligible as a source in AI Overviews?
options: An AI text file at the root of the site
To be indexed and eligible to be shown with a snippet in Google Search
A Google Ads campaign on the same query
exercises.answer: Google says there are no extra requirements: the page must be indexed and eligible for a snippet, and the usual SEO best practices apply. No special markup or file is needed, and ads have no effect on organic results.

exercises.q: Put the steps in order to publish a new guide in WordPress with its SEO settings.
steps: Write the content in the block editor with one H1 and clear H2s
Add the images with alt text in the Media Library
Choose the category and check the URL slug
Set the SEO title, meta description and indexing in Yoast or Rank Math
Publish, then view the source to check title, canonical and robots
Request indexing in Search Console with URL inspection
exercises.answer: Content first, then images and URL, then the SEO box; once live, check the real HTML (Ctrl+U) and ask Google to index it. Requesting indexing is optional: a page linked from the site and listed in the sitemap is found anyway, only more slowly.

exercises.q: Your manager wants 200 AI-written pages in one week to “rank on every keyword”. What do you do?

choices.label: Explain the risk: mass pages made to rank, without value, are spam for Google
choices.feedback: Google’s spam policies call it scaled content abuse; it can hurt the whole site, not only the new pages.

choices.label: Say yes and publish them all on Friday
choices.feedback: Unread, near-identical pages risk a manual action or a ranking drop for the whole site.

choices.label: Refuse to use AI at all
choices.feedback: Using AI is not the problem; Google judges whether the content helps people.

choices.label: Pick the 15–20 queries with real demand, draft with AI, add our data and an expert review
choices.feedback: Fewer, better pages that answer real questions, each checked by a person, then measured in Search Console.

choices.label: Keep the 200 pages but block them in robots.txt
choices.feedback: Then they bring no traffic at all, and the work is wasted.

choices.label: Publish them on a second domain
choices.feedback: The same pages on another site are still scaled content, and you split your efforts.

exercises.answer: Say no to volume for its own sake: prioritise queries with real demand, use AI to save time on drafts, add original data and human review, publish in batches and measure clicks and conversions before writing more.

interview.q: What is the difference between crawling, indexing and ranking?
interview.a: Crawling is robots downloading pages by following links; indexing is the search engine reading and storing the page; ranking is ordering indexed pages for a query. A page with no traffic is diagnosed by finding which of those steps fails.

interview.q: robots.txt or noindex: which one removes a page from Google?
interview.a: noindex. robots.txt only blocks crawling; a blocked URL can still be indexed from links, and the robot cannot see a noindex tag on a page it is not allowed to crawl.

interview.q: What are the Core Web Vitals?
interview.a: LCP for loading (good under 2.5 s), INP for responsiveness (under 200 ms, it replaced FID in 2024) and CLS for visual stability (under 0.1), measured on real Chrome users at the 75th percentile.

interview.q: How do you choose which keywords to target?
interview.a: By intent first, then by realistic difficulty and value: I look at what the first page shows for the query, pick precise long-tail queries where we can rank and that lead to conversions, and assign one page per intent to avoid cannibalization.

interview.q: Organic traffic dropped 30 % last week. What do you check?
interview.a: Whether it is real (tracking change, seasonality, same week last year), then Search Console: which pages and queries lost clicks, indexing errors, manual actions, a recent site release (noindex, redirects, robots.txt) and whether a Google update was announced.

interview.q: How do you get good backlinks?
interview.a: By creating things people want to cite (data studies, tools, guides), digital PR, partnerships and fixing mentions that have no link. Never by buying links, which breaks Google’s spam policies.

interview.q: A page you published in WordPress does not appear in Google after two weeks. What do you check?
interview.a: In Search Console, URL inspection: is it indexed, and if not, why. Then the page source (Ctrl+U): a noindex left by the SEO plugin or by “Discourage search engines”, a canonical pointing elsewhere, the URL blocked in robots.txt. Then whether the page is in the sitemap and linked from other pages, and whether it brings something new compared with existing pages.

interview.q: How do you adapt your SEO to AI Overviews and chat assistants?
interview.a: Google says the same fundamentals apply, with no special markup. I keep pages crawlable and indexable, answer the question clearly at the top, add original data, an author and a date, structure with headings and tables, and work on brand mentions. I measure with Search Console (AI features are counted in web search), referrals from assistants in GA4 and conversions, and I keep an eye on Google’s official pages because it changes fast.

interview.q: Can we use ChatGPT to write our blog articles?
interview.a: Yes, as a tool: Google accepts AI-assisted content when it is helpful and reliable. A person must check the facts, add our experience and data and edit the text. What is not acceptable is mass-producing pages to rank without value, which Google treats as scaled content abuse.
